source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (Regional Final)
source.paper: 2019-20 Regional Final, Shuttle Round, question A1

prompt: The angles of a quadrilateral are $150^\circ$, $120^\circ$, $x^\circ$ and $y^\circ$. The ratio $x:y$ is $2:3$. Find the value of $x$.

solutions.title: Angle sum
solutions.body:
The angles of a quadrilateral sum to $360^\circ$, so $x+y=360-270=90$. With $x:y=2:3$, $x=\frac25\cdot90=36$.

**Answer: $36$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (Regional Final)
source.paper: 2019-20 Regional Final, Shuttle Round, question A2

prompt: Let $T=36$. In the quadrilateral $ABCD$, $AB=AD$ and $BD=BC$. $ABE$ is a straight line and $\angle DAB=\angle CBE=T^\circ$. $\angle BDC=x^\circ$. Find the sum of the digits of $x$.

solutions.title: Chase angles
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from A1.) Triangle $ABD$ is isosceles with apex angle $36^\circ$, so $\angle ABD=\frac{180-36}2=72^\circ$. On the straight line $ABE$: $\angle ABD+\angle DBC+\angle CBE=180^\circ$, so $\angle DBC=180-72-36=72^\circ$. Triangle $DBC$ is isosceles ($BD=BC$) with apex $72^\circ$, so $x=\angle BDC=\frac{180-72}2=54$. The digit sum is $5+4=9$.

**Answer: $9$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (Regional Final)
source.paper: 2019-20 Regional Final, Shuttle Round, question A3

prompt: Let $T=9$. David has lost some of his marbles. He started with $40T$ marbles, coloured red and blue in the ratio $5:4$. After losing some red marbles, the ratio is now $4:5$. How many red marbles did he lose?

solutions.title: Blue marbles do not change
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from A2.) He started with $360$ marbles: $200$ red and $160$ blue. The blue number stays $160$; the new ratio $4:5$ means red is now $\frac45\cdot160=128$. He lost $200-128=72$ red marbles.

**Answer: $72$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (Regional Final)
source.paper: 2019-20 Regional Final, Shuttle Round, question A4

prompt: Let $T=72$. In the quadrilateral $ADCB$ the point $E$ lies on $AD$ so that $\angle EBA=\angle BEC=\angle DCE=90^\circ$. Also $CD=16$ cm, $BC=15$ cm and $BE=\frac18T$ cm. Find the length, in cm, of $AE$. Give your answer in the form $\dfrac ab$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers with no common factor other than $1$.

solutions.title: Similar triangles
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from A3.) $BE=9$ cm. In right triangle $BEC$ (right angle at $E$), $EC=\sqrt{15^2-9^2}=12$. In right triangle $ECD$ (right angle at $C$), $ED=\sqrt{12^2+16^2}=20$.

Since $\angle BEC=90^\circ$, $\angle AEB+\angle CED=90^\circ$, so $\angle AEB=\angle EDC$ (both equal $90^\circ-\angle CED$). Hence the right triangles $ABE$ and $ECD$ are similar, and $\cos\angle AEB=\cos\angle EDC=\frac{16}{20}=\frac45$. In triangle $ABE$, $BE=AE\cos\angle AEB$, so $AE=\frac{9}{4/5}=\frac{45}4$.

**Answer: $\frac{45}4$ cm**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (Regional Final)
source.paper: 2019-20 Regional Final, Shuttle Round, question B1

prompt: The positive integer $12$ can be written as the sum of three consecutive positive integers: $12=3+4+5$. Find the largest positive integer $N$ such that $42$ can be written as the sum of $N$ consecutive positive integers.

solutions.title: Sum formula
solutions.body:
If the integers start at $a\ge1$, the sum is $Na+\frac{N(N-1)}2=42$, so $N(2a+N-1)=84$. Since $a\ge1$, $2a+N-1\ge N+1$, so $N(N+1)\le84$, giving $N\le8$. $N=8$: $84/8$ is not an integer. $N=7$: $2a+6=12$, $a=3$, and indeed $3+4+\dots+9=42$.

**Answer: $7$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (Regional Final)
source.paper: 2019-20 Regional Final, Shuttle Round, question B2

prompt: Let $T=7$. The equation $x^2-(7T-2)x+420=0$ has solutions $a$ and $b$ with $a>b$. Find $a-b$.

solutions.title: Factor
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from B1.) The equation is $x^2-47x+420=0$. Two numbers with sum $47$ and product $420$ are $35$ and $12$, so $a=35$, $b=12$ and $a-b=23$.

**Answer: $23$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (Regional Final)
source.paper: 2019-20 Regional Final, Shuttle Round, question B3

prompt: Let $T=23$. There are $T+5$ counters in a bag, coloured red and blue in the ratio $5:2$. Equal numbers of red and blue counters are added to the bag until the ratio is $3:2$. Find the number of red counters that are added.

solutions.title: Set up the ratio
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from B2.) There are $28$ counters: $20$ red and $8$ blue. Adding $k$ of each gives $\frac{20+k}{8+k}=\frac32$, so $40+2k=24+3k$ and $k=16$.

**Answer: $16$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (Regional Final)
source.paper: 2019-20 Regional Final, Shuttle Round, question B4

prompt: Let $T=16$. A bag contains $2T-2$ counters. Of these $T+9$ are red. The probability of selecting two counters at random, of which exactly one is red, is $\dfrac ab$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers with no common factor other than $1$. Find $a+b$.

solutions.title: Count
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from B3.) There are $30$ counters, $25$ red and $5$ not red. The probability of exactly one red is $\frac{25\cdot5}{\binom{30}2}=\frac{125}{435}=\frac{25}{87}$. So $a+b=25+87=112$.

**Answer: $112$**

source.paper: 2019-20 Regional Final, Shuttle Round, question C2

prompt: Let $T=12$. The volume of a cuboid is $64T\ \text{cm}^3$. Its surface area is $560\ \text{cm}^2$. The volume of a smaller but geometrically similar cuboid is $324\ \text{cm}^3$. The surface area of the smaller cuboid is $S\ \text{cm}^2$. Find $S$.

solutions.title: Scale factors
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from C1.) The big cuboid has volume $768$. The volume ratio is $\frac{324}{768}=\frac{27}{64}$, so the linear ratio is $\frac34$ and the area ratio is $\frac9{16}$. Then $S=560\cdot\frac9{16}=315$.

**Answer: $315$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (Regional Final)
source.paper: 2019-20 Regional Final, Shuttle Round, question C3

prompt: Let $T=315$. The interior angles, in degrees, of a polygon with $\dfrac{2T}{105}$ sides form an arithmetic sequence with common difference $\dfrac{4T}{105}$. Find the size, in degrees, of the smallest angle in the polygon.

solutions.title: Sum of the arithmetic sequence
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from C2.) The polygon has $6$ sides and the common difference is $12^\circ$. The angle sum is $(6-2)\cdot180=720$. If the smallest angle is $s$, the angles are $s,s+12,\dots,s+60$ with sum $6s+12(0+1+\dots+5)=6s+180=720$. So $s=90$.

**Answer: $90$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (Regional Final)
source.paper: 2019-20 Regional Final, Shuttle Round, question C4

prompt: Let $T=90$. The line with the equation $y=2x+A$ meets the circle with the equation $x^2+y^2=T$ at just one point. Find the value of $A^2$.

solutions.title: Tangent condition
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from C3.) The line $2x-y+A=0$ is tangent to the circle, so its distance from the origin equals the radius $\sqrt{90}$: $\frac{|A|}{\sqrt{2^2+1^2}}=\sqrt{90}$, so $A^2=5\cdot90=450$.

**Answer: $450$**

solutions.title: Discriminant
solutions.body:
Substitute $y=2x+A$ into $x^2+y^2=90$: $5x^2+4Ax+A^2-90=0$. One point of contact means the discriminant is zero: $16A^2-20(A^2-90)=0$, so $4A^2=1800$ and $A^2=450$.

**Answer: $450$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (Regional Final)
source.paper: 2019-20 Regional Final, Shuttle Round, question D1

prompt: A right-angled triangle has perpendicular sides $15$ and $20$. The perpendicular from the right-angle vertex to the hypotenuse has length $h$. Find the value of $h$.

solutions.title: Area in two ways
solutions.body:
The hypotenuse is $\sqrt{15^2+20^2}=25$. The area is $\frac12\cdot15\cdot20=150$, which also equals $\frac12\cdot25\cdot h$. So $h=12$.

**Answer: $12$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (Regional Final)
source.paper: 2019-20 Regional Final, Shuttle Round, question D2

prompt: Let $T=12$. The line with the equation $4y=5x+T$ meets the parabola with the equation $16y=5x^2-100-T$ at the points with coordinates $(a,b)$ and $(c,d)$. Find the value of $a+c$.

solutions.title: Eliminate y
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from D1.) Multiplying the line by $4$: $16y=20x+48$. Equating with the parabola: $5x^2-112=20x+48$, so $5x^2-20x-160=0$, i.e. $x^2-4x-32=0$. The sum of its roots is $a+c=4$.

**Answer: $4$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (Regional Final)
source.paper: 2019-20 Regional Final, Shuttle Round, question D3

prompt: Let $T=4$. A point has coordinates $(-T-3,\,1-2T)$. After reflection in the line $y=-x$, followed by a translation of $10$ units to the right and $5$ units up, it has coordinates $(a,b)$. Find the value of $a+b$.

solutions.title: Transform the point
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from D2.) The point is $(-7,-7)$. Reflection in $y=-x$ sends $(x,y)$ to $(-y,-x)$, giving $(7,7)$. Translating by $(10,5)$ gives $(17,12)$. So $a+b=29$.

**Answer: $29$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (Regional Final)
source.paper: 2019-20 Regional Final, Shuttle Round, question D4

prompt: Let $T=29$. The integer $T^2+31T+108$ has $n$ different prime factors. Find the value of $n$.

solutions.title: Factorise
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T$ was the answer passed on from D3.) $29^2+31\cdot29+108=841+899+108=1848=2^3\cdot3\cdot7\cdot11$, which has $4$ different prime factors.

**Answer: $4$**
